data.content_ref: inline:The claim asserts that 'the cost of error is minimized' by choosing the highest-empirical-content theory 'regardless of its truth probability.' But minimizing error cost is incoherent without truth probability under both standard decision-theoretic readings. (1) If 'minimized cost' means expected loss, truth probability is the indispensable weight on the loss; excluding it makes the expectation undefined. (2) If the mechanism's own framing — 'minimax strategy' — is adopted, then the worst-case loss of adopting a false theory is identical across all theories regardless of content (the loss is 'you adopted a false theory'); the maximum loss does not vary with empirical content, so minimax cannot discriminate between high-content and low-content theories. Thus 'regardless of truth probability' cannot be reconciled with 'cost of error is minimized' under either expected-loss or minimax interpretation. Additionally, the claim's stated selection criterion ('highest empirical content') is not the criterion the mechanism actually defends; the mechanism defends 'best-corroborated theory,' i.e. survival of past tests — a distinct Popperian concept. An untested theory can have maximal empirical content yet zero corroboration, so the mechanism's defense does not support the claim's stated criterion.
